Summary adjusted with SLOOS insights:
- Labor market and real activity: The FOMC’s “continued strengthening” in employment and “moderate” growth remains plausible. SLOOS shows current C&I lending standards largely unchanged for large, middle-market, and small firms, with domestic banks expecting to ease C&I standards ahead and expecting improved C&I asset quality—supportive for business credit supply and consistent with gradual growth.
- Inflation: Still below 2% with low market-based inflation compensation; no direct SLOOS contradiction.
- Investment and credit channels: SLOOS points to tightening in riskier segments—banks expect to tighten standards on CRE (including construction/land development and nonfarm nonresidential) and on auto loans, and expect deterioration in asset quality for credit cards and autos. Foreign banks report weaker business-loan demand and expect tighter standards for C&I and CRE. These factors align with the FOMC’s note that business fixed investment is “soft” and suggest headwinds in capex tied to CRE and in consumer durables (autos).
- Household credit: Some easing expected for residential mortgages (GSE-eligible and nonconforming jumbo) and little change for GSE-eligible/HELOCs; this offsets some tightening elsewhere and can support housing-related spending, consistent with improved consumer sentiment.
- Policy stance: Given mixed credit conditions—easing for core C&I and some mortgages but tightening for CRE and autos with consumer-credit quality concerns—the FOMC’s “gradual” path and continued reinvestments remain appropriate to sustain accommodative financial conditions.

Net effect on tone: Still cautiously positive, but SLOOS adds notable pockets of tightening and asset-quality concerns that temper the outlook for investment and some consumer credit. Slightly less positive than before.
